papers.what_it_establishes: Cross-platform verification of whether two modules prepare the same state, using an inter-module two-qubit gate to get sub-exponential scaling versus the exponential scaling of classical-communication-only randomized-measurement protocols. Demonstrated on a six-qubit flip-chip device (two three-qubit modules).
papers.overlap_reason: Prior art for hardware measurement of state-overlap/moment quantities using an explicit entangling operation between registers -- structurally the family the material's destructive SWAP test belongs to. Its question is cross-module agreement between two preparations; the material's is absolute purity against a pre-registered prediction, with the failure of that prediction as the result. Nothing on drift, readout characterization, or pre-registration.

papers.title: Systematic Characterization of Transmon Qubit Stability with Thermal Cycling
papers.authors: Cong Li, Zhaohua Yang, Xinfang Zhang, Zhihao Wu, Shichuan Xue, Mingtang Deng
papers.what_it_establishes: Longitudinal characterization of 27 tunable transmons over one year across four thermal cycles. Establishes a hierarchy of stability: intrinsic parameters (qubit frequency, baseline T1) are robust to thermal stress (frequency deviations within ~0.5%, non-degraded coherence baselines), while environmental variables (background flux offsets, the microscopic TLS landscape) undergo significant stochastic reconfiguration after each cycle. Introduces a 'T1 Spectral Topography Fidelity' metric and concludes thermal cycling is a 'hard reset' of the local defect environment, injecting spectral randomization equivalent to thousands of hours of continuous low-temperature evolution; the noise realization is statistically distinct for each cycle.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the closest published analogue to the material's cross-session finding. It independently establishes exactly the hierarchy the material reports — the slow within-run drift is small, but the between-epoch reconfiguration is large and stochastic, on identical hardware. It therefore substantially pre-empts the QUALITATIVE claim that 'same circuits, same physical qubits, different session' is a different noise realization. It does NOT overlap on: (i) the drift being measured in a derived quantity (purity) rather than T1/flux/TLS spectra, (ii) the ~20x within-vs-cross ratio being quantified, (iii) cross-session without a thermal cycle (the material's sessions are cloud jobs, not cooldowns — an important and defensible distinction the paper should make explicitly), or (iv) the n=3/n=4 ordering flip. Cite it, and distinguish 'cross-cooldown' from 'cross-session on a live device'.

papers.title: Predicting quantum teleportation fidelity on noisy hardware with multi-channel noise modeling and experimental validation
papers.authors: Tanvir Hassan, Asif Akhtab Ronggon, Pranon Ghose, A. K. M. Nurnobi, Nur Mohammod Jim, Aparajita Datta
papers.what_it_establishes: Density-matrix simulation framework for teleportation with physically motivated noise channels calibrated to contemporary superconducting processors, explicitly modeling readout misassignment, coherent control errors, leakage, crosstalk and low-frequency dephasing. Produces an end-to-end error budget, validates predictions against experimental executions with bootstrap confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and goodness-of-fit analysis, and reports close agreement between predicted and measured behaviour. Concludes readout misassignment is the dominant fidelity limiter and that targeted readout mitigation has higher leverage than equivalent coherence improvements.
papers.overlap_reason: Methodologically the nearest neighbour in the whole search: same predict-then-measure-then-attribute loop, same statistical apparatus (bootstrap CIs), same headline conclusion that readout is the dominant limiter and that fixing the readout input is worth more than fixing coherence. This substantially weakens any claim that 'readout dominates and closes the gap' is a new finding. What it does NOT do: the predictions are not pre-registered (the model is calibrated to the device, so agreement is a fit, not a locked-in miss); the observable is teleportation fidelity, not state purity via a SWAP test; there is no cross-session drift analysis; and readout crosstalk is modeled generically rather than measured as an excitation-weight-resolved, saturating function. The material's defensible edge over it is the pre-registration and the drift result, NOT the readout attribution.

papers.title: Detecting and tracking drift in quantum information processors
papers.authors: Timothy Proctor, Melissa Revelle, Erik Nielsen, Kenneth Rudinger, Daniel Lobser, Peter Maunz, Robin Blume-Kohout, Kevin Young
papers.what_it_establishes: A fast, statistically sound spectral-analysis technique for resolving time dependence in quantum processors, applicable to time-series data from any QIP experiment. Establishes that the most widely used characterization tools assume static error rates, and that this mismatch causes unheralded failures, misidentified error modes and wasted experimental effort. Demonstrated on simulations and trapped-ion experiments across randomized benchmarking, gate set tomography and Ramsey spectroscopy; detects instability, localizes its source, applies drift control and shows the instability suppressed.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the standard-setting prior art for the material's entire drift framing, and the sentence 'static-error assumptions cause unheralded failures and misidentified error modes' is essentially the material's thesis stated in 2020. Any referee will expect it cited. Overlap is PARTIAL rather than DIRECT because the method is a spectral test on time-series from characterization protocols (RB/GST/Ramsey) on trapped ions with full device access, whereas the material has a cloud device, no per-job calibration metadata, three coarse sessions, and measures drift in a derived state property. The material's within-vs-cross-session magnitude comparison is not something this paper performs.

papers.title: Reliable Devices Yield Stable Quantum Computations
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.venue_year: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE) 2023
papers.what_it_establishes: Relates device reliability to computation stability by quantifying differences in the statistical distributions of characterization metrics collected at different TIMES AND LOCATIONS using Hellinger distance, then validates an analytical bound relating that distance directly to the stability of a computed expectation value. Demonstrated in numerical simulation with models informed by the ibm_washington transmon device; the stability metric is consistently bounded above by the Hellinger distance, castable as a tolerance level.
papers.overlap_reason: Same authors as the two Dasgupta & Humble works the material already cites, but this specific paper is the one that formalizes exactly the material's core logical move: non-stationary device characteristics propagate to instability in a computed observable, with a quantitative bound. The material's ~1% per-qubit within-session drift propagating to ~0.01 in purity is an empirical instance of this bound. Distinctions: their demonstration is a numerical simulation informed by device models rather than a hardware measurement, they use Hellinger distance on distributions rather than a derived state quantity, and they say nothing about readout misspecification or cross-session reconfiguration. Add this to the existing Dasgupta & Humble citations — omitting it while citing the other two would look selective.

papers.title: Mitigating measurement errors in multiqubit experiments
papers.authors: Sergey Bravyi, Sarah Sheldon, Abhinav Kandala, David C. McKay, Jay M. Gambetta
papers.what_it_establishes: Classical post-processing mitigation of measurement errors under two noise models: tensor-product and CORRELATED Markovian (CTMP). Error rates parameterizing these models are extractable from calibration data by a simple formula; mitigation applies the inverse noise matrix to the outcome probability vector. Overhead is exponential in epsilon*n. Experimentally demonstrated on IBM devices with stabilizer measurements for graph states up to n=12 and 20-qubit entangled states from low-depth random Clifford circuits.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the canonical establishment that multiqubit readout errors are CORRELATED rather than tensor-product, and that the correlations are extractable from calibration data and invertible. It pre-empts any claim that 'readout errors are correlated' is itself news. The material's genuine increment over it is empirical and specific: the magnitude on this device (P(1|0) rising 1.6% -> 16.9%), the fact that the dependence SATURATES with excitation weight rather than accumulating (which is a statement about the structure of the correlation, not merely its existence, and is not what the CTMP generator assumes), and the use of the measured correlation to close a pre-registered prediction gap. Frame the contribution as characterization-on-an-opaque-platform, not as discovery of correlated readout error. Did not appear in the seed's citation graph; found by targeted search.

papers.title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing
papers.authors: Seungchan Seo, Joonwoo Bae
papers.what_it_establishes: Verifies measurement readout errors in IBM AND RIGETTI cloud quantum services through quantum detector tomography, identifying and quantifying 'measurement crosstalk errors' in multiqubit measurements. Reports that entanglement is found as a source of crosstalk errors in a three-qubit measurement.
papers.overlap_reason: The single most uncomfortable hit for the readout half of the material: it characterizes measurement crosstalk specifically on CLOUD services, specifically including Rigetti, by detector tomography, and specifically finds that the crosstalk depends on the correlated state being measured. That is close to the material's excitation-dependent readout finding, on the same vendor's hardware, four years earlier. It does not report the 1.6%->16.9% magnitude, the saturation-with-weight structure, the discrepancy against a published specification, or anything about purity, drift or pre-registration — but the paper cannot claim novelty for 'readout crosstalk exists on cloud Rigetti hardware and detector tomography reveals it'. Did not appear in the seed's citation graph; found by targeted search.

papers.title: I Know What You Are Reading: Evaluating Readout Crosstalk in Cloud-based Quantum Computers
papers.authors: Y. H. Tan, Jakub Szefer
papers.venue_year: Proceedings of the 2025 Quantum Security and Privacy Workshop (ACM), 2025
papers.what_it_establishes: Evaluates readout crosstalk on commercial, cloud-based superconducting quantum computers (prior work having used experimental systems not publicly available), reconstructs the likely shared readout feed-line architecture and identifies which readout resonators share a feed line, and shows that crosstalk-induced readout errors let an adversary infer the state of co-located victim qubits, causing information leakage.
papers.overlap_reason: The physical content — one qubit's readout outcome depends on the excitation state of neighbouring qubits, measurably, on a commercial cloud device — is the same effect the material reports, arrived at from the security side. It also does the frequency-multiplexing/feed-line reconstruction that would explain WHY the material's correlation saturates with weight (shared feed line, finite resonator response) rather than accumulating. The material should engage with this mechanism explicitly. It does not quantify the effect as a per-weight readout-error model, does not feed it back into a physical prediction, and has nothing on purity, drift or pre-registration.

papers.title: Model validation and error attribution for a drifting qubit
papers.authors: Malick A. Gaye, Dylan Albrecht, Steve M. Young, Tameem Albash, N. Tobias Jacobson
papers.what_it_establishes: Argues that reporting single-value qubit metrics fails to account for the low-frequency noise processes that make those values drift, and shows that the DISTRIBUTION of repeated randomized-benchmarking error rates can validate or invalidate candidate noise models — a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on the RB error-rate distribution suffices to rule out noise models, provided the experiment spans long enough to capture the relevant low-frequency noise. Warns that error attribution using the distribution of drifting RB error rates requires care.
papers.overlap_reason: Directly relevant to the material's 'seven candidate mechanisms were bounded or excluded' step. It establishes the accepted statistical standard for excluding noise models under drift, and specifically cautions that error attribution in the presence of drift is easy to get wrong. The material's mechanism-exclusion argument will be judged against this. Also independently supports the material's critique of single-value published specifications. It does not treat readout error, correlated readout, purity, or cloud/provenance issues.

papers.title: Trust, but Verify: Preregistered Assurance for Quantum Results — A Helium VQE Testbed Across Two IBM Heron Processors
papers.authors: Amit Brahmbhatt (Quantum Clarity LLC)
papers.venue_year: Zenodo, self-deposited, record dated 28 June 2026 (record type: dataset)
papers.what_it_establishes: Per the Zenodo record description: a methodology for validating VQE computations through cryptographically frozen contracts — physical invariants (variational energy lower bound, particle-number conservation, spin-projection conservation) declared BEFORE execution, serialized to JSON and fixed by SHA-256 hash, with results receiving auditable ACCEPT/FLAG/ABSTAIN verdicts against the immutable contract, demonstrated on helium across two IBM Heron processors.
papers.overlap_reason: IMPORTANT CAVEAT ON RELIABILITY: this is a self-deposited Zenodo record from a single author at an LLC, typed as a dataset, with no peer-review indicators and zero citations. I read only the record description, not the document; I cannot vouch for its contents, quality, or that the experiment was performed as described. Treat it as a provenance flag, not as established literature. It matters because it is the ONLY item in the entire search that pre-registers hash-locked acceptance criteria before quantum hardware execution — so an unqualified 'first pre-registered quantum hardware study' claim is exposed. It differs in substance: a validity/assurance protocol producing verdicts on VQE invariants, not a locked numerical prediction of a physical observable tested to 17 standard errors, and it has no readout, drift, or provenance analysis. Recommend the paper make a narrower, defensible claim (e.g. pre-registered numerical predictions of a hardware-measured state property) rather than a categorical first.

papers.title: Error mitigation with stabilized noise in superconducting quantum processors
papers.authors: Youngseok Kim, Luke C. G. Govia, Andrew Dane, Ewout van den Berg, David M. Zajac, Bradley Mitchell, Yinyu Liu, Karthik Balakrishnan, George Keefe, Adam Stabile, Emily Pritchett, Jiri Stehlik, Abhinav Kandala
papers.what_it_establishes: Cites the seed. Shows that noise-model staleness caused by qubit-TLS resonant interactions leads to INCORRECT OBSERVABLE ESTIMATION, and that deliberately tuning qubit-TLS interactions stabilizes noise and thereby makes error mitigation more reliable. Provides a controlled platform for studying mitigation under quasi-static noise.
papers.overlap_reason: Closest prior demonstration of the material's central causal chain — a wrong input to the noise model yields a wrong predicted observable, and correcting the input restores agreement. But the wrong input there is TLS-driven gate-noise drift, not an unpublished readout parameter; predictions are not pre-registered; and the fix is a hardware intervention rather than a specification-completeness argument.

papers.title: QC-MM: A Metadata and Schema Model for Traceable Quantum-Circuit Experiments
papers.authors: Nawel Huenchuleo, Samuel Sepulveda, Alejandro Fernandez
papers.what_it_establishes: Cites the seed. A platform-agnostic JSON-Schema metadata model for quantum-circuit execution records with TIME-INDEXED CALIBRATION BINDING, transpilation traceability, provenance links, validation rules and controlled schema evolution. Evaluated on IBM Quantum Cloud and a local SpinQ NMR device; supports repeated-run statistical reporting and links compilation decisions to outcomes.
papers.overlap_reason: Directly targets the exact artifact the material could not obtain — per-job calibration metadata bound to the execution record — and frames its absence as a reproducibility failure. It is a proposal/data-modeling contribution that PRESUMES the platform exposes calibration state (IBM does). The material is the complementary empirical case where the platform does not, and where the execution path itself is unverifiable. Useful as the standards-side citation; not a novelty threat.

papers.title: Deep Neural Network Discrimination of Multiplexed Superconducting Qubit States
papers.authors: Benjamin Lienhard, Antti Vepsalainen, Luke C. G. Govia, Cole R. Hoffer, Jack Y. Qiu, Diego Riste, Matthew Ware, David Kim, Roni Winik, Alexander Melville, Bethany Niedzielski, Jonilyn Yoder, Guilhem J. Ribeill, Thomas A. Ohki, Hari K. Krovi, Terry P. Orlando, Simon Gustavsson, William D. Oliver
papers.what_it_establishes: Neural-network state discriminators on a 5-qubit frequency-multiplexed superconducting device reduce assignment error by up to 25% and reduce READOUT CROSSTALK by up to one order of magnitude, by compensating system-dependent nonidealities.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes that neighbour-induced readout crosstalk in multiplexed readout is a first-order, order-of-magnitude effect and is mitigable at the discrimination layer. Supports the material's magnitude (1.6% -> 16.9%) as physically ordinary rather than anomalous, which cuts against framing the crosstalk size itself as a discovery.

papers.title: Robust shadow estimation
papers.authors: Senrui Chen, Wenjun Yu, Pei Zeng, Steven T. Flammia
papers.what_it_establishes: Adds an experimentally friendly calibration stage to Huang-Kueng-Preskill shadow estimation, giving an UNBIASED classical shadow under noise with minimal assumptions on experimental conditions, with rigorous sample-complexity bounds and numerical demonstrations.
papers.overlap_reason: The material's single-copy shadow anchor miss (predicted 1.500 +/- 0.028, measured 1.344) is precisely the readout-induced bias that this protocol calibrates away. A referee will ask why robust/calibrated shadows were not used, or will read the anchor miss as a re-derivation of a known bias. The material should pre-empt this explicitly: its point is that the bias is invisible if you build the prediction from the published spec, not that the bias was unknown.

papers.title: Cross-Platform Verification of Intermediate Scale Quantum Devices
papers.authors: Andreas Elben, Benoit Vermersch, Rick van Bijnen, Christian Kokail, Tiff Brydges, Christine Maier, Manoj Joshi, Rainer Blatt, Christian F. Roos, Peter Zoller
papers.what_it_establishes: Protocol measuring state overlaps and PURITIES from randomized local product-basis measurements plus classical communication, enabling fidelity of separately prepared mixed states across platforms; demonstrated by measuring experiment-theory fidelities for entangled 10-qubit states on a trapped-ion simulator.
papers.overlap_reason: Prior art for hardware measurement of purity / second moments and for comparing a measured moment against a theoretical value across devices. Differences: trapped ions, randomized measurements rather than a destructive SWAP test, no readout-error diagnosis, no pre-registration, and the comparison is a verification tool rather than a falsification test of a published specification.

papers.title: Simulation and Benchmarking of Real Quantum Hardware
papers.authors: T. Piskor, M. Schondorf, M. Bauer, D. Smith, T. Ayral, S. Pogorzalek, A. Auer, M. Papic
papers.what_it_establishes: Cites the seed. Presents a noise model evaluated on superconducting hardware, benchmarks it by simulating a 20-qubit superconducting quantum computer, and claims improved overall prediction accuracy versus comparable literature models.
papers.overlap_reason: Shares the material's methodology — build a noise model, predict hardware outcomes, score the prediction — but scores models against each other for accuracy rather than treating a single locked prediction as a falsifiable hypothesis. No pre-registration, no diagnosis of which omitted input caused a miss, and no readout crosstalk or purity content.

papers.title: A Preparation Nonstationarity Loophole in Superconducting-Qubit Bell Tests / Preparation nonstationarity in superconducting-qubit Bell tests
papers.authors: Prosanta Pal, Shubhanshu Karoliya, Gargee Sharma, Ramakrishna Podila
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint Jan 2026; published Phys. Rev. A 114, 012446 (2026)
papers.what_it_establishes: THE SEED. Argues the i.i.d. assumption behind Bell tests -- that repeated circuit executions sample one stationary preparation ensemble -- is violated on current superconducting hardware. Introduces an ensemble-divergence framework giving a relaxed bound |S| <= 2 + 6*delta_ens, and an operational witness delta_op from bin-resolved outcome statistics. On IBM ibm_fez and ibm_torino with Pauli-axis measurements, finds statistically significant operational drift that PERSISTS after full two-qubit readout mitigation (assignment-matrix inversion, condition number ~20-24), which they use to argue the drift is preparation-side rather than a measurement artifact. Compares round-robin (interleaved) vs blocked scheduling: blocked schedules amplify drift into measurable ensemble divergence.
papers.overlap_reason: Shares the material's core thesis shape -- that hardware nonstationarity breaks an assumption an experiment's interpretation silently rests on -- and is the nearest published framing of 'drift as a loophole, not a nuisance.' But the results are close to complementary rather than duplicative. The seed's headline is that drift SURVIVES readout mitigation; the material's headline is the opposite direction: once readout (6.5%/qubit, ~3x assumed) and its excitation-dependent crosstalk are actually measured and fed back, the prediction gap essentially closes (0.7163 predicted vs 0.7184 measured). The seed also has no pre-registration, uses IBM (a directly-routed vendor cloud, not a brokered subnet), measures a CHSH/Pauli-axis drift witness rather than a purity/moment observable, and has no cross-session-vs-within-session decomposition. This is a must-cite, and arguably the paper to position against, not a novelty threat.

papers.title: Modeling and mitigation of cross-talk effects in readout noise with applications to the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
papers.authors: Filip B. Maciejewski, Flavio Baccari, Zoltan Zimboras, Michal Oszmaniec
papers.what_it_establishes: Introduces a correlated measurement-noise model capturing multiqubit readout cross-talk while staying efficiently describable, plus 'Diagonal Detector Overlapping Tomography' to characterize k-local measurement correlations with O(k*2^k*log N) circuits. Experiments on 15- and 23-qubit devices give error reductions of >22x and 5.5x. Notably reports that the measurement-noise correlations do NOT follow the physical layout of the device.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the strongest prior art against the material's correlated-readout finding, and it is NOT in the seed's bibliography (the seed cites the 2020 uncorrelated paper instead) -- so it is a genuine one-hop-out catch. It already establishes that a qubit's readout error depends on the state of other qubits and that this is k-local and characterizable. The material therefore cannot claim to have discovered neighbour-dependent readout error. What I could NOT find here (or anywhere) is the material's specific quantitative structure: P(1|0) rising 1.6% -> 16.9% with neighbour excitation, and the correlation SATURATING with excitation weight rather than accumulating, with the operational consequence that it must be measured at each weight. I read only the abstract-level page; whether the full text contains a weight-saturation observation is unresolved and should be checked directly before claiming novelty on that point.

papers.title: Benchmarking the quality of multiplexed qubit readout beyond assignment fidelity
papers.authors: Andras Di Giovanni, Adrian Skasberg Aasen, Juergen Lisenfeld, Martin Gaerttner, Hannes Rotzinger, Alexey V. Ustinov
papers.what_it_establishes: Argues directly that assignment fidelity -- the standard published readout metric -- is an incomplete characterization because it only probes preparation of computational basis states. Proposes detector tomography for full multiqubit characterization and a 'rate of infidelity convergence' as a validation tool. Finds agreement with assignment fidelity for separable two-qubit states (implying divergence elsewhere), and reports that qubit readout correlations are not caused by significantly reduced state distinguishability.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the published version of the material's central diagnostic claim -- that the readout number a vendor publishes is not the number you need. It weakens any framing of 'specifications omit the parameter that matters' as a new insight; that argument already exists in print and is exactly this paper's title. What the material adds is the consequence: a pre-registered prediction missing by >17 SE, and the omitted parameter being the one that closes the gap. Cite this and narrow the claim accordingly. One of only two papers that cite the seed's readout reference set alongside the seed itself.

papers.title: Detecting and tracking drift in quantum information processors
papers.authors: Timothy Proctor, Melissa Revelle, Erik Nielsen, Kenneth Rudinger, Daniel Lobser, Peter Maunz, Robin Blume-Kohout, Kevin Young
papers.what_it_establishes: Spectral methods for detecting, tracking and characterizing time-dependent (non-Markovian, drifting) errors in quantum processors directly from circuit outcome time series. The canonical reference for treating drift as a first-class, measurable object rather than a caveat. 95 citations; cited by the seed.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes the detection and tracking of drift from outcome data, which covers the material's within-session ~1%/qubit drift as an already-solved measurement problem. It does not establish the material's specific and more striking claim -- that cross-session drift on BYTE-IDENTICAL circuits on the SAME physical qubits is ~20x larger than within-session drift, i.e. that the dominant instability lives between sessions, not inside them. That decomposition is the part I could not find in this line.

papers.title: Characterizing the Reproducibility of Noisy Quantum Circuits
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.what_it_establishes: Directly assesses reproducibility of a noisy circuit as the Hellinger distance between repeated computational results, then shows that device characterization data yields an ANALYTIC BOUND on that observed variability. Validated on an ensemble of single-qubit test circuits on a superconducting transmon processor with well-characterized readout and gate error rates; the composite device parameter is confirmed to upper-bound the observed Hellinger distance.
papers.overlap_reason: NOT currently cited by the material, and it should be. This is the closest published statement of 'published device characterization predicts run-to-run irreproducibility' -- the same logical move the material makes when it feeds measured readout back to reproduce the observed purity. The material's differences are real: a physical purity observable rather than a distribution distance, multi-qubit registers rather than single-qubit test circuits, cross-session rather than repeat-within-characterization, and a device whose characterization data was NOT available (which is precisely the condition under which this paper's bound cannot be applied). That last point is a good hook: the material is arguably the negative-space case for this paper.

papers.title: Impact of Unreliable Devices on Stability of Quantum Computations
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.venue_year: ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing (2024); arXiv 2023
papers.what_it_establishes: Derives and validates bounds on the stability of a 5-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani implementation from device-characterization similarity metrics. Using ibm_washington noise data spanning January 2022 to April 2023, finds the reliability metric fluctuating between 41% and 92%, far exceeding the 2.2% threshold needed for stable outcomes -- concluding the device was unreliable for reproducing the statistical mean.
papers.overlap_reason: NOT currently cited by the material (the material cites the 2021/2022 Dasgupta-Humble papers, not this one). This is the strongest published quantitative statement that long-baseline device instability dominates and breaks reproducibility on real hardware, and it is the natural anchor for the material's ~0.2-in-purity cross-session finding. It is characterization-data-driven and simulation-propagated rather than a direct hardware re-execution of identical circuits on identical qubits, which is where the material adds something. Referees who know this line will expect it cited.

papers.title: Model validation and error attribution for a drifting qubit
papers.authors: Malick A. Gaye, Dylan Albrecht, et al.
papers.what_it_establishes: Title, venue and date confirmed via OpenAlex; abstract NOT read. Title indicates model validation and attribution of error to specific mechanisms for a qubit undergoing drift.
papers.overlap_reason: On title alone this is the closest match to the material's 'seven candidate mechanisms bounded or excluded' methodology -- attributing an observed drift to a specific cause rather than reporting it. Worth reading in full before the material claims novelty for its mechanism-elimination procedure. Reported as a lead, not a verified finding.

papers.title: Modeling and mitigation of cross-talk effects in readout noise with applications to the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
papers.authors: Filip B. Maciejewski, Flavio Baccari, Zoltán Zimborás, Michał Oszmaniec
papers.what_it_establishes: The canonical characterization of CORRELATED readout noise on cloud superconducting hardware. Introduces a k-local correlated measurement-noise model and Diagonal Detector Overlapping Tomography (O(k·2^k·log N) circuits), with experiments on 15 IBM qubits and 23 Rigetti qubits. Reports an unexpected structural finding: the measurement-noise correlations do NOT correspond to the physical layout of the device. Reports mitigation gains (error reduction factors >22 on IBM, >5.5 on Rigetti).
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes that a qubit's readout error depends on other qubits' states, on both IBM and Rigetti, five years before the material — so 'readout errors are correlated' is NOT novel and must be cited as established. What the abstract and the Quantum journal page do not contain, and what I could not find anywhere: the specific functional dependence the material reports (P(1|0) rising 1.6% -> 16.9% between idle and excited neighbours) and, more importantly, the finding that the correlation SATURATES with excitation weight rather than accumulating, which is what forces per-weight measurement. Maciejewski's k-locality is an assumption about how many qubits participate, not a measured saturation law in excitation weight. The material's contribution should be framed as the weight-resolved shape of the effect, not its existence.

papers.title: Characterizing the Reproducibility of Noisy Quantum Circuits
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.what_it_establishes: Defines reproducibility of a noisy circuit as the Hellinger distance between computational results across repeated executions, and shows that well-characterized readout and gate error rates give an UPPER BOUND on the observed variability. Validated on an ensemble of single-qubit test circuits on a superconducting transmon processor.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the existing formal treatment of the material's 'drift propagates into the observable' claim, and it is by the same group already cited (dasgupta2021stability / dasgupta2022assessing) but is a DIFFERENT paper that appears not to be in the material's bibliography. It should be added. Distinctions: single-qubit circuits only, so no entangled-register purity; it bounds variability from characterized error rates rather than testing a locked prediction; and the abstract gives no within-session vs cross-session decomposition, which is where the material's ~1% vs ~0.2-in-purity (roughly twenty-fold) contrast lives.

papers.title: Impact of Unreliable Devices on Stability of Quantum Computations
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.venue_year: ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing (2024); arXiv Jul 2023
papers.what_it_establishes: Derives necessary conditions for generating stable results within a given tolerance and tests them on IBM Washington using noise data spanning January 2022 to April 2023 with a 5-qubit implementation. Reports the reliability metric fluctuating between 41% and 92% against a maximum allowable threshold of 2.2% needed for stable outcomes, concluding the device was unreliable for consistently reproducing the statistical mean.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes, quantitatively and over 15 months, that day-to-day device instability vastly exceeds the tolerance a user needs — which is the general form of the material's cross-session finding. The material must not claim that 'devices are unstable across sessions' is new. What remains open: this is a bitstring-distribution reliability metric on a 5-qubit circuit, not a purity/moment observable; there is no byte-identical-circuit same-physical-qubit controlled comparison isolating cross-session from within-session drift; and there is no nested-register ordering flip.

papers.title: Fast Fingerprinting of Cloud-based NISQ Quantum Computers
papers.authors: Kaitlin N. Smith, Joshua Viszlai, Lennart Maximilian Seifert, Jonathan M. Baker, Jakub Szefer, Frederic T. Chong
papers.venue_year: IEEE International Symposium on Hardware Oriented Security and Trust (HOST), 2023; arXiv Nov 2022
papers.what_it_establishes: A fast method to fingerprint cloud-based quantum computers and identify WHICH machine a job ran on, across IBM's fleet of 25 superconducting transmon devices, using unique qubit frequency characteristics derived from current and historical calibration data. Reports good inter-device separation and intra-device stability, with enrollment and recall requiring minimal executions.
papers.overlap_reason: Directly addresses the material's most exposed methodological weakness — that the execution path of an individual job through the Bittensor/Open Quantum routing layer cannot be independently verified. Prior art establishes that device identity IS empirically recoverable from a handful of circuits. A referee will ask why this was not applied. The material should cite it, state plainly that it was not run (pre-registered protocol, no further runs possible), and note that its own cross-session non-monotonicity is exactly the signature one would want a fingerprint to disambiguate. Note the abstract does NOT address adversarial or untrusted providers — it is a characterization tool, not an attestation protocol.

papers.title: Quantum Volume in Practice: What Users Can Expect From NISQ Devices
papers.authors: Elijah Pelofske, Andreas Bärtschi, Stephan Eidenbenz
papers.what_it_establishes: Independent user-side quantum volume measurements on 24 NISQ devices across five providers (IBM Q, IonQ, Rigetti, Oxford Quantum Circuits, Quantinuum), finding that QV values achieved in their tests typically LAG BEHIND officially reported results, and attributing much of the gap to compilation effort and qubit-subset selection.
papers.overlap_reason: The published precedent for the material's framing that vendor-reported figures overstate what an ordinary cloud user obtains. The material must cite this rather than presenting spec-versus-measured divergence as a new observation. Distinctions: Pelofske et al. attribute the gap to compilation and qubit selection, not to a MISSING specification entry; they do not measure readout error, purity, or session-to-session variation. The material's sharper claim — that the single wrong input is precisely the one the specification does not publish — is not made here.

papers.title: Trust, but Verify: Preregistered Assurance for Quantum Results — A Helium VQE Testbed Across Two IBM Heron Processors
papers.authors: Amit Brahmbhatt (Quantum Clarity LLC)
papers.venue_year: Zenodo self-deposit, 28 June 2026, v1.0 — NOT peer-reviewed
papers.what_it_establishes: Cryptographically freezes (SHA-256) a pass/fail decision contract before observing results — three physical invariants: an energy lower bound of 1.6 mHartree, electron-number conservation +/-0.05, and spin-projection conservation +/-0.05 — then applies the single pre-committed contract across five scenarios on two IBM Heron r2 processors (ibm_kingston, ibm_fez), yielding ACCEPT / FLAG / ABSTAIN / ABSTAIN / FLAG. Framed as methodological validation of an auditable trust mechanism, not a physics result.
papers.overlap_reason: The only item found that pre-registers quantitative pass/fail criteria for a quantum hardware result in the way the material does, including a hash-locked commitment. REPORTED WITH A STRONG CAVEAT: this is a self-deposited, non-peer-reviewed Zenodo record from a single author at a private LLC, surfaced via OpenAlex alongside a cluster of similarly self-deposited items of unclear quality. It should not be cited as authority, but the material should not claim absolute priority on hash-locked pre-registration without acknowledging it exists. Different observable (VQE energy invariants, not purity), different platform, and it reports verdicts rather than a prediction miss in standard-error units.

papers.title: Probing Context-Dependent Errors in Quantum Processors
papers.authors: Kenneth Rudinger, Timothy Proctor, Dylan Langharst, et al.
papers.what_it_establishes: CITED BY SEED. Framework for detecting errors whose rate depends on circuit context rather than being an intrinsic property of the operation.
papers.overlap_reason: Context-dependence is the general category the material's finding belongs to: readout error on one qubit depending on the excitation state of its neighbours is a context-dependent error. This paper owns the concept and the detection framework; it does not report the specific spectator-excitation readout dependence. Title verified via Crossref.

papers.title: Mitigating measurement errors in multiqubit experiments
papers.authors: Sergey Bravyi, Sarah Sheldon, Abhinav Kandala, David McKay, Jay Gambetta
papers.what_it_establishes: Two classical post-processing schemes for measurement-error mitigation, based on tensor-product and on correlated Markovian noise models, with error rates extracted from calibration data by a simple formula. Demonstrated on IBM devices with graph states up to 12 qubits and 20-qubit entangled states.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes correlated readout noise modeling and the practice of folding measured readout rates back into an observable estimate — the operation the material performs when it moves the prediction 0.89 -> 0.75. Highly cited (355) baseline that a referee will expect to see. Does not address spectator-excitation dependence specifically or drift.

papers.title: Benchmarking the quality of multiplexed qubit readout beyond assignment fidelity
papers.authors: Andras Di Giovanni, Adrian Skasberg Aasen, Juergen Lisenfeld, Martin Gaerttner, Hannes Rotzinger, Alexey V. Ustinov
papers.venue_year: Phys. Rev. Applied 24, 044043 (2025); arXiv February 2025 (second hop)
papers.what_it_establishes: Argues assignment fidelity is an incomplete characterization of readout because it only probes computational basis state preparation; uses detector tomography instead, proposes rate of infidelity convergence as a fuller benchmark, and reports that qubit readout correlations are NOT induced by reduced state distinguishability, so correlation coefficients are themselves a useful optimization tool.
papers.overlap_reason: Directly pre-empts part of the material's critique that vendor specifications omit the load-bearing readout parameter: the argument that the standard readout figure of merit is insufficient is already published. The material's version is stronger (the spec omits readout error entirely, not merely reports the wrong summary of it), but the conceptual point is not new.

papers.title: Classical shadows for non-iid quantum sources
papers.authors: Leonardo Zambrano
papers.what_it_establishes: CITES SEED. Standard classical shadow guarantees rely on experimental rounds being i.i.d., an idealization violated in practice by parameter drift, environmental noise and active feedback, which generate history-dependent sequences. Introduces a robust shadow protocol using a truncated mean estimator and proves its sample complexity for the time-averaged state or channel matches standard i.i.d. shadow-norm scaling even when rounds depend arbitrarily on the past.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the theory paper for exactly the failure mode of the material's single-copy shadow anchor (predicted 1.500 +/- 0.028, measured 1.344 over 9000 snapshots on a drifting device). It establishes both that drift breaks the i.i.d. assumption underlying shadows AND that a fix exists. The material's shadow miss should be interpreted against this rather than presented as an unexplained anomaly, and the paper answers 'what is the estimator even converging to' — the time-averaged state. Five months old, found only via the citation graph.

papers.title: Robust Shadow Estimation
papers.authors: Senrui Chen, Wenjun Yu, Pei Zeng, Steven T. Flammia
papers.what_it_establishes: Sample-efficient, noise-resilient shadow estimation protocol with an experimentally friendly calibration procedure that characterizes and mitigates noise in the shadow scheme under minimal assumptions, retaining approximately standard sample efficiency with provable noise resilience.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes that shadow estimation on noisy hardware requires and admits a calibration step. The material's uncalibrated shadow anchor miss (1.500 predicted vs 1.344 measured) is the outcome this protocol exists to prevent, so a referee will ask why calibrated shadows were not used. Since no further runs are possible, this needs a limitations paragraph rather than a rebuttal.

papers.title: Whole-device entanglement in a 65-qubit superconducting quantum computer
papers.authors: Gary J. Mooney, Gregory A. L. White, Charles D. Hill, Lloyd C. L. Hollenberg
papers.what_it_establishes: CITES SEED. Prepared native graph states on ibmq_manhattan (65q) and ibmq_rochester (53q) and applied quantum readout-error mitigation (QREM); detected connected entanglement graphs spanning each full device. QREM increased observed entanglement in all measurements, raising detected entangled pairs on rochester from 31 to 56 of 58 connected pairs.
papers.overlap_reason: Prior art for measuring a state-quality quantity on a cloud superconducting device and showing that readout mitigation materially changes the answer — the same 31-to-56 style jump the material reports as 0.89 -> 0.75 -> 0.7163. Different quantity (entanglement witness vs purity) and no pre-registration, but it establishes that 'readout mitigation dominates the measured value' is a known effect.

papers.title: Detecting crosstalk errors in quantum information processors
papers.authors: Mohan Sarovar, Timothy Proctor, Kenneth Rudinger, Kevin Young, Erik Nielsen, Robin Blume-Kohout
papers.what_it_establishes: CITES SEED. Rigorous definition of crosstalk errors and a model-independent operational definition; protocol for detecting a large class of crosstalk errors by finding conditional dependencies between observed experimental probabilities, with at most cubic and usually quadratic scaling in qubit number. Demonstrated in simulation on 2- and 6-qubit processors.
papers.overlap_reason: Provides the canonical operational definition under which the material's finding — measurement outcomes on one qubit conditionally dependent on the state of others — is a crosstalk error, and a published protocol for detecting exactly that conditional dependence. The material's per-weight measurement is an instance of this framework.

papers.title: Characterizing mid-circuit measurements on a superconducting qubit using gate set tomography
papers.authors: Kenneth Rudinger, Guilhem J. Ribeill, Luke C. G. Govia, Matthew Ware, Erik Nielsen, Kevin Young, Thomas A. Ohki, Robin Blume-Kohout, et al.
papers.what_it_establishes: CITES SEED. Quantum instrument linear gate set tomography (QILGST) for characterizing measurements as quantum instruments; applied to dispersive measurement on a transmon in a multiqubit system. By varying delay between measurement pulse and subsequent gates, explores residual cavity photon population's effect on measurement error; reports total error 8.1 +/- 1.4%, readout fidelity 97.0 +/- 0.3%, and asymmetric output state fidelities of 96.7 +/- 0.6% (measuring 0) vs 93.7 +/- 0.7% (measuring 1).
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes both that measurement error is far larger than headline readout fidelity suggests and that it is asymmetric between the 0 and 1 outcomes — the same asymmetry the material attributes to T1 decay during readout. Prior art for 'the published readout number understates the real measurement error'.

papers.title: Characterizing the Reproducibility of Noisy Quantum Circuits
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.what_it_establishes: Directly assesses reproducibility of a noisy quantum circuit via Hellinger distance between repeated executions, and asks how device characterization metrics bound circuit reproducibility. Cited by the seed and by ~33 later works.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes the framework 'characterization metrics -> bound on reproducibility' that the material's prediction-vs-measurement test instantiates. But it bounds reproducibility from characterization the authors themselves perform; it does not test a VENDOR-PUBLISHED specification, and it is not pre-registered.

papers.title: Reproducibility in Quantum Computing
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.venue_year: 2021 IEEE Computer Society Annual Symposium on VLSI (ISVLSI), pp. 458-461
papers.what_it_establishes: Assesses NISQ reproducibility by focusing specifically on the error mechanism arising during NOISY READOUT, using an ASYMMETRIC channel for binary readout, and derives an analytic bound on Hellinger distance between outputs for different readout parameters.
papers.overlap_reason: The single closest seed reference to the material's core mechanism: it already singles out asymmetric readout as the reproducibility-limiting channel. The material's contribution beyond it is empirical and quantitative (6.5% measured vs 2% assumed; asymmetry in the T1 direction; excitation-correlated component), and the closed loop back to a corrected prediction. Should be cited; the material's framing must not claim asymmetric readout as the novel identification.

papers.title: Modeling noisy quantum circuits using experimental characterization
papers.authors: Megan Dahlhauser, Travis S. Humble
papers.what_it_establishes: A test-driven approach decomposing an application circuit into bootstrapped subcircuit experiments on a NISQ device, generating a composite noise model for the original circuit. Motivated explicitly by the difficulty of validating circuits given fluctuating noise sources.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the seed's reference #1 and the closest prior instance of 'build a noise model, predict a circuit outcome, compare to hardware.' Crucial difference: the model inputs come from the authors' OWN characterization, not from a published device specification, so the paper cannot exhibit the material's central failure mode (the missing spec input). NOTE: the seed's rendered bibliography credits this to 'Lilly, M. N. and Humble'; the published version is under Dahlhauser.

papers.title: Reliable Devices Yield Stable Quantum Computations
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.venue_year: IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE), 2023
papers.what_it_establishes: Addresses how TEMPORAL AND SPATIAL variations in noise relate device reliability to computation stability, quantifying differences between characterization distributions collected at different TIMES AND LOCATIONS via Hellinger distance, and validates an analytical bound linking the two.
papers.overlap_reason: The closest published precedent for the material's within-session vs cross-session comparison, because it explicitly separates temporal from spatial variation. It does not, from what I can verify, report the ratio of cross-session to within-session variation on byte-identical circuits on fixed physical qubits, which is the material's specific quantitative claim.

papers.title: Computational Performance Bounds Prediction in Quantum Computing with Unstable Noise
papers.authors: Jinyang Li, Samudra Dasgupta, Yuhong Song, Lei Yang, Travis S. Humble, Weiwen Jiang
papers.venue_year: IEEE Transactions on Computer-Aided Design of Integrated Circuits and Systems, 2025
papers.what_it_establishes: Predicts fidelity performance bounds for quantum programs under unstable (non-stationary) device noise, motivated by job scheduling and system management in quantum-centric supercomputing.
papers.overlap_reason: Cites the seed. Same essential move as the material (predict a hardware performance number in advance), but the prediction is a bound under an unstable-noise model, is not pre-registered, and is not tested by diagnosing a missing specification input.

papers.title: Implementation and Readout of Maximally Entangled Two-Qubit Gates Quantum Circuits in a Superconducting Quantum Processor
papers.authors: Viviana Stasino, P. Mastrovito, Carlo Cosenza, Anna Levochkina, Martina Esposito, Domenico Montemurro, Giovanni Piero Pepe
papers.venue_year: Journal of Superconductivity and Novel Magnetism, 2025
papers.what_it_establishes: On a 5-qubit transmon processor, compares circuits of increasing complexity up to maximally entangled two-qubit states, arguing the readout technique and its analysis are a key determinant of measured processor performance.
papers.overlap_reason: Cites the seed and is the closest citing work to the material's object of study (Bell-state preparation on superconducting hardware where readout dominates the assessed output). Differs in that it does not predict a value in advance, does not measure crosstalk-conditioned readout, and reports no cross-session comparison.

papers.title: Towards Redefining the Reproducibility in Quantum Computing: A Data Analysis Approach on NISQ Devices
papers.authors: Priyabrata Senapati, Zhepeng Wang, Weiwen Jiang, Travis S. Humble, Bo Fang, Shuai Xu, Qiang Guan
papers.what_it_establishes: Collects DAILY model-training and execution data on NISQ devices and shows a correlation between quantum-ML test accuracy and the device's calibration data over time, arguing that reproducing results on the SAME hardware becomes a problem as noise varies with time.
papers.overlap_reason: Second hop (cites Dasgupta & Humble Entropy 2022). This is the closest published day-to-day, same-hardware irreproducibility study. It does not separate within-session from cross-session variance, uses ML accuracy rather than a physical observable, and has no pre-registration.

papers.title: Measuring the capabilities of quantum computers
papers.authors: Timothy Proctor, Kenneth Rudinger, Kevin Young, Erik Nielsen, Robin Blume-Kohout
papers.what_it_establishes: Across twelve processors, shows that STANDARD ERROR METRICS inferred from random/disordered circuit behavior DO NOT accurately predict the performance of useful structured programs, which fail up to an order of magnitude earlier.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the strongest general prior art for the material's headline result. The claim 'headline device numbers do not predict what your circuit actually does' is established here at scale and in a top venue. The material's distinct contribution must therefore be narrowed to WHICH input fails (readout, absent from the spec) and to the pre-registered, closed-loop correction, not to the bare fact of prediction failure.

papers.title: Establishing trust in quantum computations
papers.authors: Timothy Proctor, Stefan Seritan, Erik Nielsen, Kenneth Rudinger, Kevin Young, Robin Blume-Kohout, Mohan Sarovar
papers.what_it_establishes: Converts an algorithm's circuits into closely related 'mirror circuits' whose success rates can be measured efficiently, letting a user quantify how accurately a machine executed their algorithm without classical simulation.
papers.overlap_reason: The canonical published answer to 'how do I trust hardware I do not control,' which is exactly the material's Bittensor/Open Quantum predicament. It certifies execution FIDELITY, not execution PROVENANCE (it cannot tell you which operator ran the job), so the material's provenance concern is not resolved by it, but a referee will expect the contrast to be drawn.

papers.title: Understanding Side-Channel Vulnerabilities in Superconducting Qubit Readout Architectures
papers.authors: Satvik Maurya, Chaithanya Naik Mude, Benjamin Lienhard, Swamit Tannu
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint, May 2024 (no journal venue verified)
papers.what_it_establishes: Shows that on multiplexed readout architectures an 'attacker' qubit's |0>->|1> bit-flip probability is measurably influenced by the STATE OF NEIGHBOURING 'victim' QUBITS, enough to infer the victim's output state with >80% accuracy in some qubit mappings.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the closest published statement of the material's crosstalk MECHANISM: readout flip probability conditioned on neighbours' excitation. I read the ar5iv full text and confirmed it does NOT characterize how the effect scales with the NUMBER of excited neighbours and does NOT report saturation versus accumulation. So the mechanism is prior art; the weight-dependence and saturation appear to be the material's own.

papers.title: Observable-Conditioned Backaction in Dynamic Circuits: A Higher-Order Context-Conditioned Kernel for Local Dynamics
papers.authors: Petr Sramek
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint, March 2026 (revised April 2026; single author, no venue)
papers.what_it_establishes: Argues that standard device metrics including T1, T2 and READOUT ASSIGNMENT ERROR and pairwise crosstalk are insufficient to capture measurement disturbance on spectator qubits, and introduces a context-conditioned kernel for higher-order, globally context-dependent dependencies, with IBM hardware harnesses and Zenodo artifacts.
papers.overlap_reason: The closest published argument that readout assignment error and pairwise crosstalk metrics are the wrong order of description and that CONTEXT (the state of the rest of the register) must be measured. This is conceptually the same claim as the material's 'correlation saturates with excitation weight, so it must be measured at each weight.' Different setting (mid-circuit measurement backaction on spectators, not final readout assignment), single-author unrefereed preprint. Must be read in full before the material claims the insight is new.

papers.title: Quantum Volume in Practice: What Users Can Expect From NISQ Devices
papers.authors: Elijah Pelofske, Andreas Baertschi, Stephan Eidenbenz
papers.what_it_establishes: From the title and citation context, an independent user-side evaluation of Quantum Volume on cloud NISQ devices, framed as what users actually obtain rather than what is advertised. I did NOT read the abstract or body.
papers.overlap_reason: Potentially the closest prior art for 'independently measured performance falls short of the vendor-advertised headline figure,' which is the material's rhetorical core. FLAGGED AS UNVERIFIED: I recovered only title, authors and venue from OpenAlex. This paper must be read before the material claims priority on the vendor-claim-versus-user-measurement contrast.

papers.title: Characterizing the Reproducibility of Noisy Quantum Circuits
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.what_it_establishes: Directly assesses circuit reproducibility via Hellinger distance between repeated computational results, then shows that DEVICE CHARACTERIZATION supplies an analytic UPPER BOUND on the observed variability. Validated on an ensemble of single-qubit test circuits on a superconducting transmon processor 'with well-characterized readout and gate error rates', yielding a composite device parameter that bounds the observed Hellinger distance.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the material's central question with the OPPOSITE PREMISE, and I could not find it among the three Dasgupta/Humble items the material already cites -- it should probably be added. Dasgupta & Humble show that when readout error IS well characterized, device characterization predicts reproducibility. The material shows the complementary failure: when the published specification OMITS readout (Cepheus-1-108Q publishes only 99.1% CZ / 99.9% 1Q), prediction fails by >17 standard errors, and feeding the MEASURED readout plus crosstalk back in closes the gap to 0.7163 vs 0.7184. The material is a negative-space instance of their positive result, which makes it a strong contrast citation rather than a redundancy.

papers.title: Fast Fingerprinting of Cloud-based NISQ Quantum Computers
papers.authors: Kaitlin N. Smith, Joshua Viszlai, Lennart Maximilian Seifert, Jonathan M. Baker, Jakub Szefer, Frederic T. Chong
papers.venue_year: arXiv Nov 2022 (also IEEE HOST 2023 per common listing -- venue NOT independently verified)
papers.what_it_establishes: Using current and historical calibration data from 25 IBM fixed-frequency transmon machines spanning a few months to ~2.5 years of age, shows that transmon qubit FREQUENCY characteristics form a unique, fast-to-acquire hardware fingerprint with excellent inter-device separation and intra-device stability.
papers.overlap_reason: Supplies the technical rebuttal to the material's unverifiability caveat: individual cloud devices ARE distinguishable from cheap measurements, so 'we cannot verify the execution path' is a choice of protocol rather than a hard limit. It is also indirectly reassuring for the material's cross-session comparison -- the paper's finding of high INTRA-device stability of frequency fingerprints is what would let a future run confirm 'same physical qubits' independently of the provider's claim. Different object of study (identity, not output variability).

papers.title: Experimental Evaluation of NISQ Quantum Computers: Error Measurement, Characterization, and Implications
papers.authors: Tirthak Patel, Abhay Potharaju, Baolin Li, Rohan Basu Roy, Devesh Tiwari
papers.venue_year: SC20: Int. Conf. for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis (2020)
papers.what_it_establishes: Self-described as the first systematic and rich experimental evaluation of IBM Quantum Experience devices, motivated by the observation that NISQ errors 'affect the fidelity and REPRODUCIBILITY of the program execution' and that understanding of these machines and their error characteristics is limited.
papers.overlap_reason: The single most relevant thing the SEED cites, and the template the material is following: an independent experimental characterization of a cloud NISQ platform whose error behaviour is under-documented. The material is the Rigetti-via-decentralized-broker analogue, done four device generations later, with two features Patel et al. lack -- pre-registered predictions locked to version control before submission, and a specific closed-loop mechanism attribution (readout + excitation-correlated crosstalk reconciling 0.89 -> 0.7163 against 0.7184 measured). Patel et al. characterize errors; the material tests a prediction and diagnoses why it failed.

papers.title: Measurement Crosstalk Errors in Cloud-Based Quantum Computing
papers.authors: Seungchan Seo, Joonwoo Bae
papers.what_it_establishes: Verifies, by direct quantum detector tomography on the IBMQ and RIGETTI cloud services, that measurement crosstalk errors exist; characterizes and quantifies noise in multi-qubit measurement; remarks that ENTANGLEMENT appears as a source of crosstalk error in a three-qubit measurement.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes on the material's own vendor platform (Rigetti, via cloud) that readout crosstalk is real and detectable. The entanglement observation is close to the material's Bell-state setting, where the correlated readout is measured on an entangled register. Much smaller scope (3 qubits, tomography-based, no excitation-weight scaling law, no comparison against a published specification), so it establishes existence rather than the material's quantitative structure.

papers.title: Impact of unreliable devices on stability of quantum computations (SEED)
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.venue_year: ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing, 2024 (arXiv v1 Jul 2023, v3 Jul 2024)
papers.what_it_establishes: Defines device 'reliability' as a necessary condition for stable outcomes within a tolerance, derives and validates stability bounds for a 5-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani circuit, and evaluates them against 16 months of IBM Washington calibration archives (Jan 2022 - Apr 2023). Reliability metric swung between 41% and 92% against a 2.2% threshold, so the device was judged unreliable for reproducing the statistical mean. Critically for the material: the paper's own noise-source breakdown finds SPAM (measurement) is the single largest contributor to device unreliability.
papers.overlap_reason: Same thesis family — a published device is not stable enough to reproduce its own results, and measurement/SPAM is the dominant term. But the method is a simulation driven by archived vendor calibration data, not a live pre-registered hardware run: no purity or moment measurement, no independently measured readout, no readout-crosstalk characterization, no locked-before-submission prediction, and no register-size non-monotonicity. It bounds stability from published metadata; the material's whole point is that the published metadata omits the term that mattered. This is the natural anchor citation and the paper the material must differentiate itself from in its first paragraph.

papers.title: Modeling and mitigation of cross-talk effects in readout noise with applications to the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
papers.authors: Filip B. Maciejewski, Flavio Baccari, Zoltán Zimborás, Michał Oszmaniec
papers.what_it_establishes: Introduces a correlated (k-local) measurement-noise model that can be efficiently characterized and mitigated, using Diagonal Detector Overlapping Tomography with O(k 2^k log N) circuits built from random combinations of X and identity gates. Applied on 15 IBM qubits and 23 Rigetti qubits, reducing errors by factors >22 and >5.5 respectively. Reports that readout-noise correlations do NOT follow the physical layout of the device. Cited as [46] by the seed.
papers.overlap_reason: This is the closest prior art to the material's readout-crosstalk result and the single biggest novelty risk. Its DDOT probe — random X/identity patterns — is precisely the experiment that measures how one qubit's assignment error depends on whether neighbours are excited, so the QUALITATIVE effect (P(1|0) rises with excited neighbours) is established prior art, not new. What I could NOT verify: whether the body reports the excitation-WEIGHT dependence and its saturation, which is the material's specific structural claim. HIGH-PRIORITY ACTION: read the full Quantum 5, 464 text and its 43 forward citations before claiming the saturation behaviour is new. Its 'correlations do not match device layout' finding also partly pre-empts any geometric framing.

papers.title: Mitigating measurement errors in multi-qubit experiments
papers.authors: Sergey Bravyi, Sarah Sheldon, Abhinav Kandala, David C. McKay, Jay M. Gambetta
papers.what_it_establishes: Correlated measurement-error models (tensored and continuous-time Markov / CTMP) whose rate parameters are extracted from measurement calibration data by a closed-form formula, with classical post-processing mitigation validated on IBM devices up to 20 qubits. Cited as [44] by the seed.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes the standard machinery for representing and correcting correlated multi-qubit readout error, which is the machinery the material implicitly uses when it feeds measured crosstalk back into the prediction. It does not make the material's argument (that the required inputs are absent from the vendor specification), does not measure purity, and does not test prediction accuracy prospectively. Cite as the accepted correlated-readout baseline.

papers.title: Systematic characterization of transmon qubit stability with thermal cycling
papers.authors: Cong Li, Zhaohua Yang, Xinfang Zhang, Zhihao Wu, Shichuan Xue, Mingtang Deng
papers.what_it_establishes: Longitudinal characterization of 27 frequency-tunable transmons over one year across four thermal cycles. Establishes a stability HIERARCHY: intrinsic parameters (qubit frequency, baseline T1) are robust to thermal stress (frequency deviations within 0.5%, coherence baselines undegraded), whereas environmental variables — background flux offsets and the TLS defect landscape — undergo significant stochastic reconfiguration after each cycle, equivalent to thousands of hours of continuous low-temperature evolution. Concludes the noise realization is statistically distinct per cycle and automated recalibration is necessary.
papers.overlap_reason: The closest physical prior art to the material's cross-session >> within-session drift result, and it supplies a candidate MECHANISM (TLS reconfiguration) for why byte-identical circuits on the same physical qubits give ~0.2 purity swings between sessions while within-session drift is ~0.01. Two clear gaps the material fills: it works at the device-parameter level, not the circuit-outcome level, and per the abstract it does NOT compare within-session against cross-session variation. This paper should be cited as the mechanism-side companion and used to bound one of the seven candidate mechanisms.

papers.title: Improving probabilistic error cancellation in the presence of non-stationary noise
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble
papers.what_it_establishes: Uses Bayesian adaptive estimation to stabilize probabilistic error cancellation under non-stationary noise, demonstrated on a 5-qubit Bernstein-Vazirani circuit on ibm_kolkata, giving 42% better accuracy and 60% better stability than non-adaptive PEC.
papers.overlap_reason: A forward citation of the seed and the same authors as the material's existing dasgupta2021stability/dasgupta2022assessing citations. Establishes that stale characterization degrades mitigated predictions and that adaptivity is the accepted remedy — which is precisely the remedy unavailable to the material, since per-job calibration metadata was not provided by the access path. Cite it to motivate why the material's access conditions make the standard fix impossible.

papers.title: Reproducible coherence characterization of superconducting quantum devices
papers.authors: Corey Rae H. McRae, Gregory M. Stiehl, Haozhi Wang, Sheng-Xiang Lin, Shane A. Caldwell, David P. Pappas, Josh Mutus, Joshua Combes
papers.what_it_establishes: Argues that optimization of superconducting device performance is only possible if metrics can be accurately compared across measurements, devices and laboratories, and that such comparisons are 'currently inaccurate or impossible due to understudied errors from a plethora of sources'. A reporting-standards perspective for qubit and resonator error analysis. Cited as [35] by the seed.
papers.overlap_reason: The canonical prior statement that published superconducting device metrics are not sufficient for cross-comparison — the general form of the material's specific finding that the published Cepheus-1-108Q spec omits readout error. It is a perspective/standards piece about coherence metrology in the lab, not about cloud-brokered access or predicting a circuit outcome from a spec sheet. Cite as the precedent for the disclosure argument.

papers.title: Modeling noisy quantum circuits using experimental characterization
papers.authors: Megan L. Dahlhauser, Travis S. Humble
papers.what_it_establishes: A test-driven approach to characterizing NISQ programs: bootstrapped experiments characterize individual subcircuits, which are composed into a noise model for the full circuit; accuracy is validated by total variation distance between predicted and experimental results across multiple circuit instances. Cited as [25] by the seed.
papers.overlap_reason: The established template for exactly the material's reconciliation step — build a noise model from independently measured characterization, then compare predicted against measured circuit outcomes. Two differences carry the material's novelty: the prediction here is fitted post hoc from subcircuit characterization rather than locked before submission, and the failure is not attributed to a specific undisclosed vendor parameter. The material should present its 0.89 -> 0.75 -> 0.7163 reconciliation as this method run in a pre-registered direction.

papers.authors: Kenneth Rudinger, Timothy Proctor, Dylan Langharst, Mohan Sarovar, Kevin Young, Robin Blume-Kohout

papers.title: Detection of temporal fluctuation in superconducting qubits for quantum error mitigation
papers.authors: Yuta Hirasaki, Shunsuke Daimon, Toshinari Itoko, Naoki Kanazawa, Eiji Saitoh
papers.what_it_establishes: CITES THE SEED. Continuously monitors qubit output on a superconducting quantum computer and finds STEP-LIKE changes in error rates that recur, each step persisting for several minutes. Correlates increased errors with anomalous variance of the output and builds a post-selection error-mitigation scheme on that signal.
papers.overlap_reason: Directly prior on the material's WITHIN-session drift observation (~1% per qubit). Establishes that intra-session instability on a minutes timescale is real, detectable from output statistics alone, and actionable. It does not establish the material's central comparison — within-session vs cross-session on byte-identical circuits on the SAME physical qubits — and reports no purity or readout characterization. The material's ~20x separation between the two timescales is not foreclosed by this paper, but its within-session half is.

papers.title: Trustworthy Computing using Untrusted Cloud-Based Quantum Hardware
papers.authors: Suryansh Upadhyay, Swaroop Ghosh
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint, 2 May 2023 (v1); 14 November 2024 (v2); related journal version in Frontiers in Computer Science 2024
papers.what_it_establishes: Models a future ecosystem in which untrusted, less-trusted, or unreliable vendors offer QPUs at varied price/performance points, and users are drawn to the cheaper and more available but less trusted hardware. Models adversarial tampering with results and proposes splitting shots across hardware options, plus a run-adaptive split heuristic exploiting temporal quality variation to identify untrustworthy hardware at runtime.
papers.overlap_reason: Anticipates the economic structure the material actually operated inside — a free/cheap tier routed through operators with unverified quality — and is the canonical citation for 'cheap tier implies weaker trust.' But its concern is deliberate result tampering, not specification incompleteness or drift, and it uses simulation of adversarial behaviour rather than a measured hardware campaign. It does not address whether a legitimate but opaque path degrades a scientific measurement.

papers.title: Reproducible Builds for Quantum Computing
papers.authors: Iyán Méndez Veiga, Esther Hänggi
papers.what_it_establishes: Generalizes the reproducible-builds definition to the quantum setting under two threat models: confidentiality of user data during circuit preparation and submission, and INTEGRITY OF QUANTUM COMPUTATION RESULTS. Shows three examples of hiding classical information in transpiled circuits and two cases where minimal circuit modifications produce incorrect results.
papers.overlap_reason: Establishes that the submission pipeline between user source and executed circuit is itself an attack surface and an integrity risk — relevant because the material's circuits traversed an extra mediation layer (aggregator plus distributed operators) before execution. Shows a circuit can be minimally altered en route with material effect on results. However it is a threat-model and toolchain paper with no hardware campaign, no drift analysis, and no engagement with vendor specification completeness.

papers.title: Rethinking Reproducibility in the Classical (HPC)-Quantum Era: Toward Workflow-Centered Science
papers.authors: Anna Vrtiak, Duuk Baten, Ariana Torres-Knoop
papers.what_it_establishes: Position paper arguing that scientific knowledge now depends on computational processes where hardware and software layers influence outcomes, and that quantum computing at low technological maturity amplifies existing reproducibility challenges while creating new ones through probabilistic outputs, hardware-specific noise, and tight software-hardware coupling. Proposes meta-workflows documenting both process abstractions and implementation contexts.
papers.overlap_reason: Conceptual framing only. Names 'infrastructure blends with the results,' which is a fair one-line description of the material's central problem, and is a reasonable citation for why quantum cloud results resist reproduction. It contains no measurement, no device access, and per my fetch does not discuss calibration metadata availability or device verification.

papers.title: 1-2-3 Reproducibility for Quantum Software Experiments
papers.authors: Wolfgang Mauerer, Stefanie Scherzinger
papers.what_it_establishes: Proposes a meta-generation mechanism producing DOI-safe, long-term, dependency-free reproduction packages from project artifacts alone. Explicitly designed so that traceability survives 'even when the quantum processor itself is no longer accessible' — i.e. it concedes that re-execution on the original device state is not achievable and substitutes artifact-level traceability.
papers.overlap_reason: The canonical prior statement that a quantum hardware result cannot be re-run into existence and must instead be made traceable through frozen artifacts. This is the accepted-practice baseline against which the material's version-controlled pre-registration is an increment — the difference being that pre-registration freezes the PREDICTION before the run, whereas 1-2-3 freezes the ARTIFACTS after it. Worth citing precisely to make that distinction explicit.

papers.title: Quantum Fidelity-per-Cost: A Metric for Evaluation of Quantum Computing Systems
papers.authors: Siddarth Shinde, Jakub Szefer
papers.what_it_establishes: A cross-provider measurement study of circuit execution fidelity over 14 cloud QPU access-path entries (12 distinct physical QPUs) across four access paths: AWS, IBM Quantum Runtime, IQM Resonance, and OQC. Reported dataset: 247 Bell-state executions at shot counts from 20 to 1000, with per-run counts and derived TVD and KL divergence. Proposes a cost-aware QFC score; finds cost-aware ranking differs from fidelity-only ranking and that billing model, not hardware, governs how the score scales with shot count.
papers.overlap_reason: Notable because it uses BELL STATES on cloud QPUs across multiple ACCESS PATHS — the same primitive and the same access-path concept as the material — and distinguishes 14 access-path entries from 12 physical QPUs, implicitly recognizing that path and device are not the same thing. But it measures output-distribution distance for a purchasing metric, not purity via SWAP test, has no predicted-versus-measured pre-registered comparison, and per my fetch does not discuss reproducibility, cross-session variation, or execution-path verification.

papers.title: Toward Live Noise Fingerprinting in Quantum Software Engineering
papers.authors: Avner Bensoussan, Elena Chachkarova, Karine Even-Mendoza, Sophie Fortz, Vasileios Klimis, Mohammad Reza Mousavi
papers.venue_year: arXiv preprint, v3 dated 10 July 2026 (arXiv ID indicates December 2025 original)

Cite as the statement of the principle; the material supplies the hardware instance.

papers.title: I Know What You Are Reading: Evaluating Readout Crosstalk in Cloud-based Quantum Computers
papers.authors: Yizhuo Tan et al. (full author list not retrieved)

papers.overlap_reason: A 2026 theory-plus-numerics account of exactly which noise events bias a randomized-measurement estimate - relevant to how the material attributes its residual. It does not treat purity or Renyi-2 per the abstract, is not a device demonstration on a named QPU, has no readout crosstalk characterization, and no session variation. The 'experimental validation on actual quantum hardware' claim came from a summarizer and I could NOT confirm it from the abstract - treat as numerics unless checked.

papers.title: Error mitigation with stabilized noise in superconducting quantum processors
papers.authors: Youngseok Kim, Luke C. G. Govia, Andrew Dane, Ewout van den Berg, David M. Zajac, Bradley Mitchell, Yinyu Liu, Karthik Balakrishnan, George Keefe, Adam Stabile, Emily Pritchett, Jiri Stehlik, Abhinav Kandala

Requires hardware-level control the material's Public-Tier access does not have.

papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Travis S. Humble

papers.title: Adaptive mitigation of time-varying quantum noise
papers.authors: Samudra Dasgupta, Arshag Danageozian, Travis S. Humble

papers.overlap_reason: Same family as the above; establishes that time-varying noise is a first-class obstacle requiring in-line re-estimation. No stability measurement of the kind the material reports.

papers.title: Computational Performance Bounds Prediction in Quantum Computing with Unstable Noise
papers.authors: Jinyang Li, Samudra Dasgupta, Yuhong Song, Lei Yang, Travis Humble, Weiwen Jiang

papers.title: Optimization of Quantum Error Correcting Code under Temporal Variation of Qubit Quality
papers.authors: Subrata Das, Swaroop Ghosh
papers.what_it_establishes: Analyzes 12 days of public calibration data from ibm_kyiv (127 qubits), plus ibm_brisbane and ibm_sherbrooke, showing Pauli-X and CNOT error rates fluctuate significantly over time and across qubits, and that fixed-distance QEC either underperforms or over-provisions depending on "the selected qubit and the error rate of the day".
